alert_pattern: [FIRING:1] us-1 : prod - RDS_CPUUtilizationAvgCriticalCore  |  [FIRING:1] us-1 : stage - RDS_CPUUtilizationAvgCriticalMedia
environment: us-1 prod core database (account 026972849384, profile `main`, us-east-1). Siblings: prod-core-rds, prod-media-rds, prod-thirdparty-rds, and the stage-*-rds2 set
_owner_direction: 2026-08-31: investigate CPUUtilization and DatabaseConnections graphs for the instance, attach both, search for the top query, and post a usage graph again after 5-10 minutes (follow_up.py does that automatically).
diagnosis_steps: The card NAMES the database: read `dbinstance_identifier` off the sub-alert labels (verified #121453 -> `stage-media-rds2`). Do NOT derive it from the alert name - the 'Core'/'Media' suffix only tells you the family, and follow_up._rds_instance_for reads this label directly for exactly that reason. Then rds_instance_summary to confirm WHICH ACCOUNT holds it, because a same-named database in another account is a real hazard. If the card carries no such label (an older card, or one VictorOps already closed and replaced with 'Automatically resolved'), fall back to matching the alert text against the instances that actually exist - never construct a name.
rds_metrics — CPU now/avg/peak plus connections, freeable memory, IOPS and queue depth over the same window. These numbers go in the thread; the graph is separate evidence, not a source to read from.
rds_metric_graph twice — CPUUtilization and DatabaseConnections, one metric per graph. CloudWatch renders them server-side, so there is no browser and no settle problem.

rds_top_queries — top SQL by db.load.avg AND the wait events. The wait events are the discriminator: `CPU` at the top means genuinely CPU-bound; `IO:DataFileRead` means it is waiting on storage; `Lock:*` means contention. Observed on stage-core-rds2 (2026-08-31): CPU 0.550, IO:DataFileRead 0.120.

rds_events — a failover, reboot, backup or parameter-group change in the window explains a CPU spike more often than a query does. The nightly backup shows up here (observed 02:11-02:12Z on stage-core-rds2).

rds_top_queries also returns the top USER, APPLICATION and DATABASE, and those identify the caller when the SQL alone does not. Observed 2026-09-10 on stage-media-rds2: top user `core_graphql_server`, top application `core-graphql-server`, top database `media_platform`, session type `client backend` - which is what turned 'the database is busy' into 'one service is calling it'.
Check #comms-noc for this instance: a database that spikes on a schedule is a known pattern, not a new incident.
resolution_steps: Post the two graphs, the numbers and the top SQL. The action is a human's — scaling an instance class, killing a query or rolling back a deploy are all decisions with cost or customer impact, and none of them is the agent's to take.
A usage graph is posted again automatically 5 and 10 minutes later (follow_up.py, kind `rds_usage`). Do not promise a re-check or ask a human to watch it.
gotchas: Performance Insights returns TOKENIZED statements — $1/$2 replace literal values, so no customer data comes back with them. Quote them as returned; never reconstruct a real query.
`db.load.avg` is average active sessions, not a percentage. 0.466 means about half a session busy on average — state what the number means or it reads as 46%.
storage on these instances is io1 with a large allocation (stage-core-rds2: 15999GB), so ReadIOPS peaks in the thousands are normal — compare against the instance's own baseline, not against zero.
A CPU alert on a Multi-AZ=false instance has no standby to fail over to; say so if it is relevant, since it changes what a human can safely do.
The SSO session expires several times a day. Every tool reports it as expired and names the profile — that is a gap to report, never a reason to estimate a metric.

A saturated database is very often ONE caller, not general load. stage-media-rds2 sat at ~99.6% CPU for over a day (2026-09-09 onward) with 26.9 of ~27 average active sessions attributed to a single user, driven by a bulk S3 ingest making a ~2s folder-tree GraphQL query per file. Report the dominant caller's share of active sessions - it decides whether scaling would help at all.

Check #comms-noc for an announced load test before calling it an incident. That same stage-media-rds2 spike had been announced in-channel the morning it started ('Starting 1 million files ingest scan and aggregate test on US-Stage ... there will be spikes'), and a separate on-call asked the channel whether workload testing was running before diagnosing.

The top query can CHANGE without the CPU changing, and that is a clue rather than noise: on stage-media-rds2 the dominant query switched from an rbac_acl permission lookup to a recursive tree_folder query at the exact minute core-graphql-server was rolled, while the CPU stayed pinned because the underlying ingest never stopped.
escalation: The database owner / aiWARE platform team; a sustained CPU-bound core database is customer-facing
example_commands: aws sso login --profile main   (for the human, when a tool reports the session expired)
alertname_note: The suffix after 'AvgCritical' names the DATABASE FAMILY, not the severity: Core -> the *-core-rds instance, Media -> the *-media-rds instance. The segment before the alertname is the ENVIRONMENT (prod / stage), so 'us-1 : stage - RDS_CPUUtilizationAvgCriticalMedia' is stage-media-rds2, not a prod database. Both parts have to be read or the investigation opens the wrong instance.

known_causes.cause: A bulk 'one million files' S3 ingest for a single org, running through core-graphql-server on aiw-stg198, issuing a burst of GraphQL calls per file including a ~2s recursive tree_folder lookup. Pure CPU saturation - IO waits were negligible on io1 storage.
known_causes.status: diagnosed and handed to the ingest owners; the recorded conclusion was that scaling the app would not help because the database was the bottleneck and a single caller was consuming all 16 vCPUs

alert_payload.summary: Postgres average CPU utilization has reached <threshold> for at least <duration>
alert_payload.description: Postgres <dbinstance> average CPU utilization has reached <threshold> for at least <duration>
alert_payload.use_it_for: `dbinstance_identifier` NAMES THE DATABASE - 'stage-media-rds2'. This replaces the whole alertname-guessing step: follow_up._rds_instance_for reads this label directly and never reaches the word-scoring fallback. Confirm the account with find_db_instance, but the identifier itself is a fact from the payload, not an inference.
alert_payload.trap: `instance: 10.11.10.157:10003` is the cloudwatch_exporter scraping the metric, NOT the database and NOT anything you can connect to. The database is `dbinstance_identifier` only. The summary's threshold ('reached 50') is the RULE's threshold, not the observed CPU - the observed value is not in this payload, so read it from CloudWatch and never quote 50 as the current usage.
alert_payload._shared: The parser now hands you these already split out, under 'sub-alerts parsed from state_message', with the FIRING ones listed first. Read them instead of re-reading the raw card. The block is only present while the incident is live — once VictorOps closes it the whole thing is replaced by 'Automatically resolved', and a block can be marked truncated, which means its missing fields are UNKNOWN rather than empty.

alert_pattern: Rekognition-ThrottledCount-High-wpsc01 (a CloudWatch alarm name, used verbatim as the alert title)
environment: GovCloud account 113765098011, us-gov-west-1, profile `us-1-gov` — assume-role from STATIC KEYS in ~/.aws/credentials [vtgovuser]. NOT SSO; do not tell anyone to run `aws sso login` for this one.
_owner_direction: 2026-08-31: the only gov-AWS alert in the same shape as the commercial ones. Screenshot it from CloudWatch, and take multiple captures across 5-10 minutes (follow_up.py kind `cloudwatch_usage` does that automatically).

cloudwatch.condition: AWS/Rekognition ThrottledCount, Sum over 300s, GreaterThanThreshold 100, 1 evaluation period, NO dimensions — it is account-wide Rekognition throttling, not one resource
cloudwatch.companion_metrics: CallCount, SuccessfulRequestCount, UserErrorCount, ServerErrorCount, ResponseTime, DetectedFaceCount, DetectedLabelCount — ThrottledCount alone says how many were refused; CallCount is what makes it a share rather than a bare number
cloudwatch.observed_incident: 2026-08-27T18:12Z OK -> ALARM. ThrottledCount ran 39,172 then 199,075 then 265,093 per 5-minute bucket, peaking at 787.8K over the following days, against a threshold of 100.
cloudwatch.gotcha: CloudWatch's own image API (get-metric-widget-image) DOES NOT WORK in this GovCloud account — it answers 'Throttling: Rate exceeded' every time, including after three retries with backoff, while the identical call in the commercial account returns a PNG. cloudwatch_metric_graph falls back to drawing the series locally from get-metric-statistics and captions it as locally drawn. Do not describe such a graph as a CloudWatch console screenshot.

diagnosis_steps: cloudwatch_alarm('Rekognition-ThrottledCount-High-wpsc01') FIRST — it reports the condition, the current state, and the recent state changes, and it says which account/region/partition it found the alarm in.

Read the state carefully: INSUFFICIENT_DATA is NOT a healthy zero. It means Rekognition published no datapoints in the window, which for this account is common between bursts. cloudwatch_metric_values distinguishes 'no datapoints' from 'zero' explicitly — quote whichever it actually says.

cloudwatch_metric_values for ThrottledCount AND CallCount over the same window. A throttle count without a call count is half the story: 200k throttles out of 2M calls and 200k out of 210k are different incidents.
cloudwatch_metric_graph for ThrottledCount (pass alarm= so it inherits the GovCloud account and region, and picks up the threshold line).
State the window you graphed. The alarm evaluates a 5-minute Sum; a 3h graph and a 5-day graph tell different stories about the same alarm.
resolution_steps: Post the numbers, the graph, and the alarm's own condition. The action is a human's: a Rekognition quota increase is an AWS support request with a cost conversation attached, and throttling caused by a runaway caller is an application decision.

Further captures at +5 and +10 minutes are posted automatically (follow_up.py, kind `cloudwatch_usage`) so the thread shows whether the burst is still climbing. Do not promise a re-check or ask a human to watch it.
gotchas: This account uses static keys assuming a role, not SSO. If a call fails with expired credentials the fix is the keys or the assume-role, NOT `aws sso login` — saying the wrong one sends the on-call engineer down a dead end.
GovCloud ARNs are `arn:aws-us-gov:` — a copied commercial ARN will not match anything here.
The alarm has no dimensions, so 'which resource is throttled' has no answer from this metric. Say that rather than implying one Rekognition endpoint is at fault.
escalation: The team that owns Rekognition usage in the gov environment; AWS support for a quota increase
example_commands: aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --profile us-1-gov --region us-gov-west-1 --alarm-names Rekognition-ThrottledCount-High-wpsc01
python -m oncall_agent.Agents.AWS_Agent.server --selftest   (RDS half; the alarm tools take a name)

alert_pattern: <region> : <env> - ALBUnhealthyHostCritical (*Summary:* Application Load Balancer app/<lb-name>/<id> has at least N unhealthy instances for at least 15m)
environment: any account/region with an ALB — uk-prod is account 026972849384 in eu-west-2, which is the first non-us-east-1 commercial region this repo touches
diagnosis_steps: Take the balancer and target group from the sub-alert LABELS - `load_balancer` (app/<name>/<id>) and `target_group` (targetgroup/<name>/<id>) are the ARN tails verbatim, which are also exactly the CloudWatch dimension values. Parsing them out of the summary text still works and is the fallback, but the labels are already split. Then alb_target_health(load_balancer=<that tail>) FIRST - healthy/registered counts per target group, and the reason for every unhealthy target.
Post the counts the way the owner asked: how many targets are healthy vs not, per target group, plus each unhealthy target's state and reason.
alb_health_graph for HealthyHostCount vs UnHealthyHostCount over the last 3h, so the thread shows whether this is new or has been flapping.

Read the REASON before forming a view: FailedHealthChecks means the target is really failing its check; RegistrationInProgress means a newly launched instance is still warming up and will likely pass on its own (observed: healthy within ~9 minutes, no action).
If every target is healthy now, say so — the alert fires on 'at least 1 unhealthy for at least 15m', so it can recover before anyone looks. Check the graph before calling it a false alarm.
resolution_steps: Post the counts, the reasons and the graph. The action stays a human's: pulling a target, rolling back a deploy or scaling the group are all decisions with customer impact.

A second look is posted automatically at +3 and +6 minutes (follow_up.py, kind `alb_health`) — a shorter cadence than the other families precisely because warm-up resolves inside that window. Do not promise a re-check.
gotchas: Do not act in the first 5-10 minutes for fresh instances; most resolve on their own
If it stays unhealthy past warm-up, check the service on the health-check port and instance system log

The CloudWatch dimension is the ARN TAIL (`app/uk-prod-fastcore-app-http/992c86a8ba9f5fb3`), not the load-balancer name. Using the name returns no datapoints, which reads as 'no data' rather than 'wrong dimension'.
uk-prod is eu-west-2. AWS_REGIONS has to include it or find_load_balancer will not see the balancer at all and will say so.
A target group with zero registered targets returns an EMPTY health list and no metrics — that is 'nothing behind the LB', not 'everything healthy'.

Observed on the real uk-prod balancer: healthy dropped 4->3 twice in 3h with the same instance flapping. Say 'flapping' only if the graph shows it — one dip and a sustained failure need different urgency.
escalation: The service owner behind the target group; infra for scaling decisions
example_commands: aws sso login --profile uk-prod   (for the human, when a tool reports the session expired)
_owner_direction: 2026-08-31: moved from the Grafana specialist to the AWS agent. Go to the load balancer itself, post how many targets are healthy vs unhealthy plus the status, and do it again after 2-3 minutes.

aws._verified: ELBv2 and CloudWatch shapes read live 2026-08-31 (in a sibling account while the uk-prod SSO session was expired)
aws.lookup: The alert summary carries the ARN TAIL — app/<name>/<id> — and that is the only place the balancer is named. find_load_balancer() takes either the tail, the bare name or a full ARN, and searches the allowed profiles/regions.
aws.tools: alb_target_health for the counts and reasons, alb_health_graph for the picture
aws.cloudwatch: namespace AWS/ApplicationELB, dimensions LoadBalancer=app/<name>/<id> (the ARN tail, NOT the name) and TargetGroup=targetgroup/<name>/<id> (the tail of the target-group ARN). HealthyHostCount and UnHealthyHostCount belong on ONE graph — same unit, and the ratio is the question.
aws.reasons: TargetHealth.Reason is the discriminator: Target.FailedHealthChecks is a real failure; Elb.RegistrationInProgress and Target.HealthCheckInProgress are warm-up that resolves itself; Target.DeregistrationInProgress is a deploy in flight. Three different threads, and the old case's 'wait for warm-up' advice only applies to the second. OBSERVED LIVE on uk-prod-fastcore-app-http (2026-08-31): Target.ResponseCodeMismatch — 'Health checks failed with these codes: [503]'. That is a FIFTH case and the important one: the instance is up and answering, the application behind it is returning 503, so 'wait for warm-up' is the wrong read and replacing the instance would not fix it.
